payload.title: IR: recognize functional groups
payload.fullNote: IR probes molecular vibrations. A vibration absorbs IR when it changes the molecular dipole moment. Useful approximate regions: alcohol O–H 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ (often broad); acid O–H 2500–3300 (very broad); C=O about 1650–1800; nitrile about 2210–2260. N–H is often near 3300, generally less broad than hydrogen-bonded OH.

visualCard.title: Infrared (IR) Spectroscopy: Hooke’s Law (Bond Strength vs. Reduced Mass) & Key Diagnostic Zones
visualCard.formula: ν̃ (cm⁻¹) ∝ √(k / μ)     →     Stronger Bond (↑ k: Triple > Double > Single) & Lighter Atoms (↓ μ: O–H > C–C) = HIGHER Wavenumber!

items.label: Requirement for IR Absorption
items.text: A vibration is IR-active ONLY if it changes the molecule’s net dipole moment (symmetric stretches of O₂, N₂, or trans-2-butene C=C are IR-inactive!).

comparison: 1° NH₂ = 2 peaks; 2° NH = 1 peak; 3° N = 0 peaks
Conjugation ↓ wavenumber by ~20–30 cm⁻¹; Ring strain ↑ wavenumber

visualCard.title: 3-Second IR Functional Group Identifier
visualCard.prompt: What signature peak do you see in the IR spectrum?

items.label: Strong Sharp Peak Around 1700–1750 cm⁻¹
items.outcome: Carbonyl (C=O) Present! Now Check 2500–3600 cm⁻¹:
items.text: + Broad 2500–3300 = Carboxylic Acid; + 2720/2820 doublet = Aldehyde; + 1650/3350 = Amide; + 1735 & C–O 1200 = Ester; Alone at 1715 = Ketone!

items.label: Broad Rounded Trough at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ (No 1700 Peak)
items.outcome: Alcohol (O–H) or Phenol!
items.text: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding creates a wide distribution of O–H bond strengths, broadening the peak into a smooth U-shape.

items.label: Conjugation vs. Ring Strain on C=O Wavenumber
items.outcome: Conjugation LOWERS ν̃ (~1685 cm⁻¹); Small Ring Strain RAISES ν̃ (~1780 cm⁻¹)
items.text: Conjugation gives C=O more single-bond character (↓ k → ↓ cm⁻¹); small 4/5-membered rings force higher s-character into the exocyclic C=O (↑ k → ↑ cm⁻¹).

payload.title: UV–visible: conjugation and energy
payload.fullNote: UV–visible absorption promotes electrons between electronic states. In many comparable conjugated pi systems, increasing conjugation lowers the transition energy and shifts absorption to longer wavelength. Photon energy obeys E=hc/λ. Beer–Lambert law is A=εlc in its linear regime. For a simple pi system, a pi → pi* excitation can promote an electron from the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) to the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO). Extended conjugation often narrows that gap in comparable systems; allowed transitions and actual spectra also depend on the molecule.

visualCard.title: UV–Visible Spectroscopy: HOMO → LUMO Gap, Conjugated Polyenes & Complementary Colors
visualCard.formula: ΔE = hν = hc/λ; A = εcl. Conjugation often lowers the relevant transition energy; there is no universal wavelength increment per double bond.

items.label: Why Conjugation Increases λ_max (Red / Bathochromic Shift)
items.text: Combining more p orbitals into a conjugated π system raises the HOMO energy and lowers the LUMO energy, shrinking ΔE so longer-wavelength (lower-energy) photons are absorbed.

items.label: Absorbed vs. Perceived Color
items.text: A compound that absorbs in the visible region (400–700 nm) appears as the COMPLEMENTARY color of the wavelength it absorbs (absorbs blue ~450 nm → looks orange/yellow).

chips: π → π* and n → π* Transitions

payload.title: Proton NMR: shift, integration, splitting
payload.fullNote: Chemical shift reports environment; integration reports relative proton count; splitting reports coupling. In simple first-order cases, coupling to n equivalent neighboring protons produces n+1 lines. Equivalent protons do not split one another. Deshielded protons appear downfield at higher ppm.

visualCard.title: ¹H and ¹³C NMR: Symmetry Equivalence, Chemical Shift (δ ppm), Integration & (n + 1) Splitting

items.label: Number of Signals = Chemically Non-Equivalent Proton Sets
items.text: Protons interchangeable by a rotational axis (C_n) or mirror plane (homotopic/enantiotopic in achiral solvent) give ONE shared signal.

items.label: Chemical Shift (δ ppm from TMS = 0 ppm)
items.text: Downfield (higher ppm, to the LEFT) = DESHIELDED by electronegative atoms (O, N, Halogens) or π-bond magnetic anisotropy (Aldehyde 9–10, Aromatic 7–8, Alkene 5–6, O–CH 3.5–4, α-C=O 2.1, Alkyl 0.9–1.5).

items.label: Integration (Area = Proton Ratio) & Spin–Spin Splitting (n + 1 Rule)
items.text: Peak area ratio gives the relative number of H atoms in each set; n non-equivalent neighboring H atoms (within 3 bonds, H–C–C–H) split a signal into (n + 1) peaks (Pascal’s triangle: 1:1 doublet, 1:2:1 triplet, 1:3:3:1 quartet).

payload.title: Proton NMR: shift, integration, splitting
payload.fullNote: Shift = neighborhood; area = population; splitting = neighbors. Upfield means lower ppm and greater shielding; downfield means higher ppm. Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is commonly assigned δ = 0 ppm. Coupling constant J is the line spacing in Hz, not the integral or chemical shift.

visualCard.title: Classic NMR Splitting Patterns & Exchangeable Proton Tricks
visualCard.prompt: What NMR pattern do you observe in the spectrum?

items.label: 3H Triplet (~1.2 ppm) + 2H Quartet (~3.5–4.1 ppm)
items.outcome: Unmistakable ETHYL Group (–CH₂CH₃)!
items.text: The CH₃ (3H) is split by 2 neighbors into a triplet (2+1=3); the CH₂ (2H) is split by 3 neighbors into a quartet (3+1=4).

items.label: 6H Doublet (~1.1 ppm) + 1H Septet (~2.5–4.0 ppm)
items.outcome: Unmistakable ISOPROPYL Group (–CH(CH₃)₂)!
items.text: Two symmetric methyls (6H) are split by 1 methine H into a doublet; the single CH (1H) is split by 6 methyl H’s into a 7-line septet.

items.label: 1H Broad Singlet That Vanishes After Adding D₂O
items.outcome: Alcohol (–OH) or Amine (–NH) Proton!
items.text: Rapid intermolecular proton exchange averages out spin-spin coupling (usually a broad singlet) and swaps –OH for NMR-silent –OD in D₂O!

payload.title: Proton NMR: shift, integration, splitting
payload.fullNote: n+1 is a limited first-order rule, not universal. Nonequivalent neighbors can give more complex patterns; exchangeable OH/NH protons often do not show the expected simple coupling. Chemical equivalence depends on symmetry and timescale. NMR requires nonzero nuclear spin. Odd-mass isotopes such as ¹H and ¹³C are active; odd-atomic-number nuclei with even mass, such as ²H and ¹⁴N, can also be active. Even-proton/even-neutron nuclei such as ¹²C and ¹⁶O have spin zero. Some active isotopes have broad or difficult signals, so activity alone does not guarantee easy detection.

visualCard.title: Using Peak Height Instead of Integral Area or Splitting by Equivalent / Same-Carbon Protons

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Saying a tall singlet has more protons than a wide multiplet based on peak height, or splitting a CH₃ group into a quartet using its own 3 protons.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Integral measures signal area, not height. The simple n+1 rule assumes first-order coupling to equivalent neighbors; magnetic equivalence and coupling patterns require more care in complex systems.

steps.label: 1. Formula constraint
steps.text: C3H6O has DBE=(2×3+2−6)/2=1. A carbonyl can account for that entire unit of unsaturation.

steps.label: 2. Add two measurements
steps.text: Suppose IR shows a ketone-like C=O band and proton NMR shows a single 6H singlet near 2 ppm. Two symmetry-equivalent methyl groups adjacent to C=O fit those data.

steps.label: 3. Challenge an alternative
steps.text: Propanal shares C3H6O and DBE=1 with acetone, and both have C=O absorption. But propanal has an aldehydic H (shown explicitly as CH at the terminal carbonyl carbon) and multiple proton environments; it does not fit the single 6H singlet. visualCard.title: Integrated Structure Elucidation Workflow: Formula/MS → IHD → IR → ¹H/¹³C NMR

items.label: Step 1: Molecular Formula, Nitrogen Rule & IHD
items.text: Calculate IHD = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2. If IHD ≥ 4, suspect a benzene ring (4 IHD). Check Mass Spec for M⁺ molecular ion and halogen M+2 isotopes (Cl = 3:1; Br = 1:1).

items.label: Step 2: Pinpoint Functional Groups by IR
items.text: Check 1650–1800 cm⁻¹ for C=O and 2500–3600 cm⁻¹ for O–H / N–H. Combine IHD + IR (e.g., 1 IHD + 1715 cm⁻¹ IR = ketone or aldehyde; 0 IHD + 3350 cm⁻¹ = saturated alcohol).

items.label: Step 3: Assemble Fragments with ¹H & ¹³C NMR
items.text: Use signal count to spot symmetry, integration to distribute H counts, chemical shift (δ) to place groups next to C=O or O, and (n + 1) splitting to connect adjacent CH_x neighbors.

comparison: IHD = (2C+2+N−H−X)/2; Odd MW = Odd # of N
Immediately tells you where the oxygen/nitrogen lives

figure.caption: Same formula, different connectivity: compare the two carbonyl isomers.

figureSteps.label: 1. Formula constraint
figureSteps.text: C3H6O has DBE=(2×3+2−6)/2=1. A carbonyl can account for that entire unit of unsaturation.

figureSteps.label: 3. Challenge an alternative
figureSteps.text: Propanal shares C3H6O and DBE=1 with acetone, and both have C=O absorption. But propanal has an aldehydic H (shown explicitly as CH at the terminal carbonyl carbon) and multiple proton environments; it does not fit the single 6H singlet. Compare every observation, not just formula and IR.

visualCard.title: Distinguishing Constitutional Isomers Using Combined IR + NMR Clues
visualCard.prompt: How do you quickly distinguish common isomer pairs on the MCAT?

items.label: 3-Pentanone vs. 2-Pentanone (Both C₅H₁₀O, 1715 cm⁻¹)
items.outcome: 3-Pentanone Has Symmetry → Only 2 ¹H Signals (6H Triplet + 4H Quartet) And 3 ¹³C Signals!
items.text: 2-Pentanone is unsymmetrical (4 ¹H signals including a 3H methyl ketone singlet at 2.1 ppm, plus 5 ¹³C signals).

items.label: Ethyl Acetate (CH₃COOCH₂CH₃) vs. Methyl Propanoate (CH₃CH₂COOCH₃)
items.outcome: Check Which Group Is at ~4.1 ppm (Bonded to –O–)!
items.text: In ethyl acetate, the 2H QUARTET is at 4.1 ppm (–OCH₂CH₃) and the 3H singlet is at 2.0 ppm; in methyl propanoate, the 3H SINGLET is at 3.7 ppm (–OCH₃)!

items.label: Aldehyde vs. Ketone Isomers
items.outcome: Aldehyde Shows a 1H Peak at 9.5–10 ppm NMR + 2720/2820 cm⁻¹ IR!
items.text: A ketone lacks the downfield 9.5 ppm aldehydic proton and the C–H Fermi doublet in IR.

payload.fullNote: A single NMR signal can represent several equivalent groups. DBE says how much unsaturation exists, not where it is. Do not force phosphorus-rich or unusual-valence formulas into this simple equation.

visualCard.title: Confusing the Base Peak (Tallest MS Peak = 100%) with the Parent Molecular Ion (M⁺•)

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Assuming the tallest peak in a mass spectrum is always the molecular weight (M⁺), or ignoring symmetry when counting ¹³C NMR peaks.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: The BASE PEAK is simply the most stable carbocation fragment (100% relative abundance, e.g., tropylium m/z 91 or acylium RCO⁺); the parent ion M⁺• is the highest m/z peak (excluding M+1/M+2 isotopes)!

visualCard.title: Unknown Metabolite Identification & Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometry

items.label: Bromine vs. Chlorine MS Isotope Signature
items.outcome: M : M+2 = 1:1 (Bromine ⁷⁹Br/⁸¹Br) vs. 3:1 (Chlorine ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl)
items.text: Twin parent peaks of equal height separated by 2 m/z units instantly prove the molecule contains one bromine atom.

items.label: Nitrogen Rule in Mass Spectrometry
items.outcome: Odd M⁺ Molecular Weight = Odd Number of Nitrogens (1, 3, 5...)
items.text: Because N is trivalent with an even atomic mass (14), a neutral organic molecule with 1 nitrogen always has an ODD molecular weight!

items.label: Benzylic Fragmentation (m/z = 91)
items.outcome: Alkylbenzenes Cleave at the Benzylic Bond → C₇H₇⁺ (m/z 91)
items.text: Forms the exceptionally stable aromatic tropylium cation (6π electrons in a 7-membered ring) as the base peak.

lessonInventory.title: IR: recognize functional groups
lessonInventory.coreRule: IR probes molecular vibrations. A vibration absorbs IR when it changes the molecular dipole moment. Useful approximate regions: alcohol O–H 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ (often broad); acid O–H 2500–3300 (very broad); C=O about 1650–1800; nitrile about 2210–2260. N–H is often near 3300, generally less broad than hydrogen-bonded OH.

lessonInventory.title: UV–visible: conjugation and energy
lessonInventory.tag: Longer wavelength means lower photon energy
lessonInventory.coreRule: UV–visible absorption promotes electrons between electronic states. In many comparable conjugated pi systems, increasing conjugation lowers the transition energy and shifts absorption to longer wavelength. Photon energy obeys E=hc/λ. Beer–Lambert law is A=εlc in its linear regime. For a simple pi system, a pi → pi* excitation can promote an electron from the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) to the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO). Extended conjugation often narrows that gap in comparable systems; allowed transitions and actual spectra also depend on the molecule.

lessonInventory.title: Proton NMR: shift, integration, splitting
lessonInventory.coreRule: Chemical shift reports environment; integration reports relative proton count; splitting reports coupling. In simple first-order cases, coupling to n equivalent neighboring protons produces n+1 lines. Equivalent protons do not split one another. Deshielded protons appear downfield at higher ppm.
